blocks.text: Hide storage behind a collection-like interface so domain code asks for objects, not queries.

A **repository** exposes `findById`, `add`, `save` and a few intention-revealing queries for one aggregate. The domain depends on that interface only. SQL, an ORM, a document store or a `HashMap` for tests sit behind it, so storage can change without touching business rules.

items: **Speaks:** the domain's language, in terms of aggregates and not tables.
**Hides:** query language, mapping, connections and caching.
**One per aggregate root,** not per table.

blocks.text: Unlike a table-shaped DAO, a repository works in aggregates and domain terms. Its interface is a port owned by the domain; the implementation is an infrastructure adapter.

walkthrough.note: Plain domain types with no persistence annotations. The identity is a typed `OrderId`, not a bare `String`.
The repository is an interface owned by the domain. Queries are named for business meaning, and absence is `Optional`, never `null`.
One adapter: a `ConcurrentHashMap`. A JDBC or JPA adapter implements the same three methods, and the sort makes results deterministic.
The service takes the interface in its constructor. It cannot see SQL, sessions or maps.
Wiring happens at the edge. Swapping the adapter changes one line and no domain code.

blocks.text: Appointment booking in a clinic system.

The scheduling rules are the valuable part: no double booking, no overlap with a doctor's leave. Rule tests must run in milliseconds, but production stores appointments in PostgreSQL through JPA. The rules talk to `AppointmentRepository.overlapping(doctor, slot)`. Unit tests use an in-memory adapter and a few integration tests run the JPA adapter against a real database.
Payoff: scheduling logic is tested without a database, and moving to a new store means writing one adapter.

lists.title: Use when
items: Domain logic must be testable without a database.
Storage technology may change, or differs per environment.
Queries repeat across services and deserve one named home.

lists.title: Avoid when
items: The app is thin CRUD over tables; the layer adds ceremony.
A framework repository already is the abstraction and you never swap it.

lists.title: Pitfalls
items: A leaky interface that returns query builders, `ResultSet` or `Map` internals.
Generic `findAll()` on huge tables, or one method per report.
Repositories per table instead of per aggregate root.

lists.title: Overuse smells
items: A repository that only forwards to `JpaRepository` with the same methods.

lists.title: Modern Java
items: Spring Data and Jakarta Data generate the implementation from an interface, so you write only the port.
Return `Optional` for single results and immutable lists or `Stream` for collections.

rows.difference: The repository is the collection the domain sees; a mapper does the object-to-row translation inside its implementation.
Active Record puts finders and save on the entity itself, tying it to storage. A repository keeps entities persistence-ignorant.
Repositories fetch and register objects; the unit of work decides when changes are flushed together in one transaction.
Pass a specification to one `find(spec)` method instead of growing the interface with a method per filter.
In hexagonal architecture a repository interface is the typical outbound port, and its implementation is a driven adapter.

entries.name: CrudRepository / JpaRepository
entries.detail: Declare an interface; Spring Data generates the implementation, including derived queries like `findByLastName`.

entries.name: jakarta.data.repository.Repository
entries.detail: Jakarta Data's `@Repository` marks an interface for the provider to implement; extending `CrudRepository` adds built-in operations.

entries.name: @Repository
entries.detail: A stereotype that marks the persistence component and translates vendor exceptions into `DataAccessException`.

entries.name: PanacheRepository
entries.detail: Hibernate ORM with Panache repository interface offering `find`, `list` and `persist` for an entity.

options.why: A collection-like, domain-worded interface over storage, with interchangeable backends.
A mapper translates between object and row shapes; this interface says nothing about mapping.
The entity does not save or find itself; a separate object holds the access.
A facade simplifies a subsystem's API; this interface exists to abstract where data lives.

exercises.scenario: A domain service loads and stores `Policy` aggregates. Tests must run without a database, and storage may move from PostgreSQL to DynamoDB next year. Business rules should not mention tables or queries.

options.why: A domain-owned, collection-like port with swappable adapters hides storage completely.
Policies would carry find and save, binding domain rules to a concrete store and forcing a database in tests.
Mapping is needed somewhere, but a mapper alone gives the domain no storage-agnostic interface to depend on.
A facade wraps a subsystem; it does not give the domain an abstraction in its own vocabulary.

exercises.prompt: Explain Repository in your own words: what does it hide, and why is it not just a DAO or a mapper?

modelAnswer.text: A repository gives the domain a collection-like interface for aggregates: find, add, save, in domain vocabulary. It hides storage technology and mapping. The domain owns the interface and infrastructure implements it. A mapper only translates shapes, and a DAO often mirrors tables rather than aggregates.

keyPoints: One per aggregate root, owned by the domain
Mapping and transactions are separate concerns
